Prevention: Carry out soil testing for presence of bacterial wilt and avoid planting in infected fields.
Uproot, dry and burn tomato stalks after harvest.
Avoid fields with history of bacterial wilts.
Practice 3-4 year crop rotation with crops from a different family, like maize and groundnuts.
Weed frequently and remove alternative hosts and volunteer plants.
Do not damage tomato plants during weeding.
Sterilize farm equipment such as knives and hoes with household bleach such as
Reduce root knot nematodes in the field which aggravate bacterial wilt problems.
Monitoring: Look for sudden wilting of the plant, often without yellowing of the leaves, in fields when there is adequate moisture.
Cut open the stem and look for water soaked tissue which later turns brown and sometimes leaves the stem hollow.
Do the ooze test - cut the stem and suspend it in water to check if there is milky ooze coming out, this is the bacteria.
Carry out direct controls as soon as the first symptoms are seen in the field.
Direct Control: Uproot all infected plants, dry and burn the stalks outside the field.
Restrictions: Chemical pesticides are not recommended for management of this disease as they are of little or no use because the disease survives in the soil
